common_name: Nocellara del Belice Olive (Sicilian Table Olive, Castelvetrano-Style)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in lean, alkaline, extremely well-drained soil in full sun; olives are highly intolerant of wet feet and need excellent drainage above all else.

directions: Plant in lean, alkaline, extremely well-drained soil in full sun. Nocellara del Belice comes from the Belice Valley of western Sicily and is the source of the large, bright green, mild, buttery table olives sold in North America as 'Castelvetrano-style' olives, prized for a sweet, almost fruity flavor with none of the sharp bitterness of many other green table olives. While excellent for eating fresh-cured, the variety also produces good quality olive oil, giving growers dual-purpose flexibility from a single tree. The tree is a strong, dependable producer well adapted to Mediterranean-climate growing conditions; harvest for table use while still green and firm, and allow appropriate curing time, since fresh olives straight off any tree are intensely bitter and inedible without curing.

common_name: Cerignola Olive (Large Mild Italian Table Olive)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in lean, alkaline, extremely well-drained soil in full sun.

directions: Plant in lean, alkaline, extremely well-drained soil in full sun. Cerignola takes its name from the town of Cerignola in the Puglia region of southern Italy and is grown for some of the largest table olives commonly available, producing plump, glossy fruit sold cured in both green and black stages with a mild, pleasant flavor and satisfyingly meaty texture that makes each olive feel substantial. The tree is vigorous and productive, well suited to warm Mediterranean-climate regions, and the large fruit size makes hand-harvesting and processing somewhat easier per volume of usable olive compared to smaller-fruited varieties. Harvest at the desired ripeness stage for green or black-cured olives, and cure appropriately, since fresh-picked olives of any variety are far too bitter to eat without proper processing.

common_name: Hojiblanca Olive (Dual-Purpose Spanish Oil and Table Olive)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in lean, alkaline, extremely well-drained soil in full sun; provide a compatible pollinizer variety for the best fruit set, since Hojiblanca benefits from cross-pollination.

directions: Plant in lean, alkaline, extremely well-drained soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer nearby. Hojiblanca, meaning 'white leaf' in Spanish for the strikingly silvery undersides of its foliage, is one of the most important olive varieties of Andalusia in southern Spain, valued for genuine dual-purpose flexibility, producing both good quality mild oil and firm, attractive table olives from the same tree depending on how the crop is used and harvested. The tree is vigorous, productive, and reasonably disease-tolerant, contributing to its widespread commercial planting across southern Spain. Harvest earlier and greener for table olive curing, or later for oil pressing, and remember that all olives require proper curing before eating fresh off the tree, since raw fruit is intensely bitter.

common_name: Empeltre Olive (Cold-Hardy Spanish Sweet Oil Olive)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in lean, alkaline, extremely well-drained soil in full sun; self-fertile, so a single tree will produce fruit, and relatively more cold-tolerant than many olive varieties.

directions: Plant in lean, alkaline, extremely well-drained soil in full sun; self-fertile, so a single tree will produce fruit. Empeltre originates in the Aragon region of northern Spain, where it has adapted to somewhat cooler conditions than many Mediterranean olive varieties tolerate, giving it a useful edge in cold hardiness for growers at the margins of olive-growing climate. The medium, dark purple-black fruit produces a mild, sweet, fruity oil low in bitterness, prized in traditional Spanish and Balearic Islands cooking, and the fruit can also be cured as a sweet, mild table olive. The tree is self-fertile and reliably productive, a practical choice for smaller home orchards wanting a single olive tree without needing a separate pollinizer variety. Cure harvested fruit properly before eating, since raw olives are far too bitter to consume fresh.

common_name: Amfissa Olive (Greek Dual-Purpose Table and Oil Olive)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in lean, alkaline, extremely well-drained soil in full sun.

directions: Plant in lean, alkaline, extremely well-drained soil in full sun. Amfissa, also known as Conservolia, is grown around the Greek town of Amfissa near Delphi and is one of Greece's most important dual-purpose olive varieties, producing large, round, mild-flavored fruit used both as a popular table olive, typically cured black and glossy, and pressed for good-quality oil when the crop or market calls for it. The tree is reliably productive and well adapted to traditional Greek Mediterranean growing conditions, and the fruit's large size and mild flavor have made it a familiar sight in Greek markets and export products. As with all olives, harvested fruit must be properly cured before eating, since fresh olives straight off the tree are intensely, unpalatably bitter regardless of variety.
